newsitem.title: CHINA: HK lawyers pile constitutional pressure on govt.
newsitem.headline: HK lawyers pile constitutional pressure on govt.

text.p: Lawyers piled pressure on Hong Kong's post-colonial government on Thursday, pushing ahead with a landmark court challenge to the legal system and arguing that the new legislature had violated constitutional rules.
Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa, meanwhile, triggered a fresh controversy with an electoral blueprint that would give votes to corporations rather than individuals in next May's elections
Tung also drew barbs in the local media over reports that aides had asked schoolchildren at a centre he had visited on Wednesday not to get too close and not to ask for his autograph.
The landmark court case went into its third day with former Bar chairwoman Gladys Li leading top lawyers in the attack on Solicitor General, Daniel Fung.

Li told the court on Wednesday Hong Kong's Provisional Legislature had violated rules set for the creation of Hong Kong's first post-colonial lawmaking body, after Britain's handover of the 156-year-old colony to China on July 1.

China set up the Provisional Legislature to replace Hong Kong's elected chamber after the handover. Members of the handpicked legislature, meeting across the border in China, passed some bills while the British were still in power.
Li said the interim body failed to meet legal rules for the first post-handover assembly as fixed by China's parliament, the National People's Congress (NPC) in 1990.
She said a Preparatory Committee appointed later by Beijing, which had crafted transitional institutions, dodged the issue by naming the assembly the Provisional Legislative Council.

But Li said: "It is set up as a legislature. It purports to fulfil the functions of a legislature. So if it is not a legislature, what is it? The Provisional Legislative Council is in fact the first legislative council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region," Li argued.
She said it did not conform with the NPC decision that the first assembly should have deputies elected from constituencies.
The provisional legislators were appointed by a 400-member selection committee tightly screened by Beijing, and the elected Legislative Council was disbanded on July 1.
Fung argued that the court has no power to rule on the legality of the provisional legislature.

But the three judges hearing the case took a different view. "It is still open to this court to question whether the Provisional Legislative Council has been established in accordance with the law," judge Barry Mortimer said.
Li's arguments were expected to face a fierce counter-attack by government counsel later on Thursday.

The drama has grown out of a criminal case in which defence lawyers argued the criminal conspiracy charges faced by their clients ceased to exist after the handover, because the new legislature had not formally adopted any pre-handover laws.
Tung has expressed confidence the government will win, but he said the it would abide by the ruling either way.
Tung is grappling with a host of problems ranging from illegal immigrant children from mainland China to anger over his rolling back of civil freedoms and labour rights laws.
Tung on Wednesday launched a proposal for "corporate voting" to elect legislators from 30 "functional constituencies".
This would reverse reforms of the last British Governor Chris Patten, who shifted from corporate to individual voting.
The popular Democratic Party angrily condemned Tung's move as a step backwards and a bid to wreck the electoral chances of the party which did well under the one-man one-vote principle.
"It is targeted against us," said Lee Wing-tat, one of the party's former legislators, ousted on July 1. "Our chance of participating in the election will be very low."

Cracks began to emerge in the provisional legislature on Thursday, with one lawmaker, Leong Che-hung, slamming the government for treating the body like a rubber stamp by asking it to rush through decisions at short notice.
